text.tspan: invalidate in-flight listings
the membership of one or two directories changes

g.text: does the source exist on the server?
Local file, not yet on the server — the atomic save

text.tspan: A running upload of this file does not get aborted —
the rename queues behind it. Aborting mid-upload can
leave half an object on the server, and for the atomic
save the ordering is the whole point

g.text: is the destination name taken locally?

text.tspan: FileIo drop the replaced file's buffer
DbWrite its eviction markers and rows
adopt the replaced file's ETag as our base version
so the upload below asserts If-Match: that version —
a safe replace that only conflicts on a *concurrent*
server change. Uploading with If-None-Match: * instead
would flag the document being replaced as a conflict
and bury the save in a conflicted copy

g.text: is the new name ephemeral too?

text.tspan: mark the buffer dirty — the file must now
exist on the server under the new name
schedule a publish on the moved object
It is scheduled, not run here: the local rename is
already committed, so a failed upload must not make
the rename report failure

g.text: Answer OK — the upload follows on its own

text.tspan: A failed upload must not fail the rename. The local
rename is already committed, so reporting failure would
tell the kernel the rename never happened while our
state says it did — and its dentry cache would stay out
of step for good. It is also the wrong answer for the
user: here EIO reads as your document could not be
saved, although the content is safe in the buffer and
only the upload is outstanding. It is retried by the
next flush, and the failure was already reported

g.text: did it replace a destination we knew?

text.tspan: FileIo drop that file's buffer
DbWrite remove its rows — mirroring
what the MOVE just did on the server

g.text: DbWrite move the row and its subtree's paths

text.tspan: Moved, not deleted and re-inserted by the reconcile
below: that keeps the inode alive, so open file handles
and a pending write buffer keyed by it survive the
rename. A dropped buffer would silently lose the edit
Net PROPFIND the old parent —
and the new one, when it differs
